title: Arizona Confirms First Clade I Mpox Case as U.S. Infections Rise
excerpt: The travel-associated case adds to more than 20 Clade I mpox infections reported across the United States since late 2024, though health officials say the risk to the general public remains low.
body:
• Arizona confirmed its first case of Clade I mpox on July 22, acquired by an individual while traveling outside the country.
  • Clade I mpox carries a mortality rate of 1-10%, significantly higher than the 1-4% rate for Clade II, which drove the 2022 U.S. outbreak.
  • More than 20 Clade I cases have been reported across the United States as of June 2026, with frequency increasing since March.
  • The JYNNEOS vaccine is expected to protect against both clades and is most effective when administered within four days of exposure.

Arizona health officials on Tuesday confirmed the state's first case of Clade I mpox, a more severe strain of the virus that has been spreading through Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023 and is now appearing with increasing frequency in the United States.

The Arizona Department of Health Services said the individual acquired the infection while traveling outside the country. There is currently no evidence of local transmission connected to the case, officials said. As of July 21, Arizona has reported 34 total mpox cases, including this Clade I infection.

Why Clade I Matters

Mpox — formerly known as monkeypox — is caused by two main genetic groups, or clades, of the monkeypox virus. Clade II was responsible for the global outbreak that began in 2022, with approximately 37,500 cases reported in the United States since then. Clade I, however, is considered more dangerous.

According to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Clade I mpox carries a mortality rate ranging from 1% to 10%, compared with less than 1% to 4% for Clade II. Clade I is also "more likely to cause severe illness and death, especially in people who are immunocompromised," the school's factsheet states.

While Clade II has been primarily transmitted through sexual contact, Clade I spreads through a broader range of pathways, including exposure to infected animals, household contact, close physical or intimate contact, and contaminated objects known as fomites.

A Growing Pattern Across the U.S.

The Arizona case is part of a broader national trend. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that more than 20 Clade I mpox cases have been confirmed in the United States as of June 2026, with frequency increasing since March. The first U.S. case was diagnosed in California in November 2024, in a traveler returning from East Africa.

All U.S. cases to date have been linked to recent international travel — either to Central and Eastern African countries at the center of the outbreak or to parts of Western Europe where newer clusters have been reported. Globally, more than 55,000 confirmed Clade I cases have been reported since January 2024, including more than 150 deaths.

"The risk posed by the clade I monkeypox outbreak to most people within the United States remains low."

— Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Vaccination and Prevention

Health officials emphasized that the JYNNEOS vaccine, a two-dose regimen, is expected to protect against both Clade I and Clade II infections. Arizona's health department urged anyone who may have been exposed to mpox to contact their healthcare provider or local health department promptly.

"Vaccination is most effective when given within four days of exposure but may still reduce illness when given within 14 days," the department said, advising people to monitor for symptoms for 21 days following their last contact with an infected individual.

The CDC discontinued routine aircraft contact tracing for all mpox clades in 2025 after investigations found low transmission risk during commercial air travel. However, the agency continues to recommend that people with active mpox infections avoid travel until fully recovered.

What Indian Americans Should Know

The development is particularly relevant for frequent travelers between the United States and South Asia, Africa, or Europe. While India has reported limited mpox cases, the virus's broader transmission dynamics and the rising number of travel-associated Clade I cases globally underscore the importance of awareness for diaspora communities with extensive international travel patterns. Health experts recommend that eligible individuals, particularly those planning travel to affected regions, consult their healthcare provider about mpox vaccination.
